### Payrolls Triple the Forecast, the Chips Bounce, and Mississippi Widens

Filed as: Edition No. 11 — The Midday Watch · 2026-11-06T12:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-06-midday-watch.html

The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Payrolls Triple the Forecast, the Chips Bounce, and Mississippi Widens

 At noon the morning has corrected the week in three places. The October payrolls report, the test the Overnight Watch left at 0830, came in at 165,000 jobs against a consensus of 59,000, with unemployment down to 4.1 percent and the two prior months revised up by 84,000. New York opened split and an hour in the chips were bouncing and the Dow was not. And the count corrected itself in the open: Mississippi’s margin is wider in the newest tally, Colorado’s 4th stands at 3,069 in the wire’s latest totals, and no race was called in the morning.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Friday, November 6, 2026. This edition continues Edition No. 10, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400. Where the noon figures differ from the overnight figures, the difference is stated here, in the open; the overnight edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

 

The Noon in Brief

The morning’s largest settled fact is a labor report, not a market move. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported at 0830, against forecasts of 59,000 in the Dow Jones consensus and 65,000 in the Reuters poll. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent from 4.2. September’s gain, first printed at 29,000 in every edition of this paper since it was released, is revised to 60,000, and August’s to 186,000. The correction is filed where corrections belong, at the top of the next edition. Around that fact the morning arranged itself: the Nasdaq bounced on chip buying and the Dow did not follow; Europe fell at its midday by more than the overnight futures had promised; Brent seesawed across $100 and back under it; gold fell for a second session; the odds of a December rate increase rose from about two in three to better than three in four; and in Washington and Moscow the official statements of the morning were, in order, a deadline reached in the House Republican leadership race and a spokesman saying there are no details.

The Payrolls: 165,000, and the Record Corrected Upward

The report beat the highest forecast on the shelf, not only the consensus. CNN’s account of the release and USA Today’s account carry the same headline figures: 165,000 jobs added in October, unemployment at 4.1 percent, and combined upward revisions of 84,000 to August and September—August up 53,000 to 186,000, September up 31,000 to 60,000. The release file adds the detail under the headline: private payrolls up 159,000 against 64,000 expected, and the unrounded unemployment rate at 4.141 percent against 4.1753 percent the month before. The three-month average gain now stands at 137,000. The September figure this paper carried at 29,000 for five weeks was the bureau’s first estimate; the bureau’s second estimate is 60,000, and the log records the change rather than quietly replacing it.

The hiring was led by the services that employ the most people. Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs, against a prior-year average of 15,000 a month in the accounts; health care added 42,000, transportation and warehousing 25,000, and manufacturing 19,000, per the market account carrying the report’s breakdown. Average hourly earnings rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38.00, and 3.1 percent over the year—the strongest monthly wage gain since January in one account, and above the 0.3 percent and 2.9 percent the forecasts had carried. The labor force grew by 421,000 and participation rose to 61.9 percent from 61.8. Two figures in the same report run the other way and are printed with the rest: the number working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million, and long-term unemployment stands at 2.0 million, 27.6 percent of all unemployed, up from about 1.1 million in 2023. The private ADP report, already in at 86,000, which the overnight edition printed as the morning’s advance bearing, pointed the right way and understated the official figure by half.

The consumers in the same morning’s second report are less cheerful than the payrolls, and the survey predates the election. The University of Michigan’s preliminary November sentiment index rose to 51.0 from October’s final 48.0, against expectations of 47.5 to 48, per Dow Jones Newswires’ account: current conditions at 51.0, up from 46.7, expectations at 50.9, up from 48.8, and one-year inflation expectations down to 4.3 percent from 4.7. The interviews ran from October 20 to November 2 and closed before Tuesday’s results were known; the final November reading, with post-election interviews in it, comes later in the month. The index stands near its record low of 44.8, set in May. The two reports together are the morning’s economic whole: the hiring is stronger than anyone forecast, and the households being hired remain, by their own account, gloomy.

The Markets’ Reading at Noon: The Chips Bounce, the Dow Does Not

New York opened in the split the futures had promised, and the first hour widened the technology side of it. At 9:36 a.m. the Nasdaq Composite was up 1.2 percent at 24,601.93 and the S&P 500 up 0.38 percent at 7,381.99, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 449.65 points, or 0.87 percent, at 51,073.41, in the market account filed above. By 10:01 the bounce had broadened inside the same split: the Nasdaq up 1.7 percent at 24,732.09, the S&P 500 up 0.9 percent at 7,421.33, and the Dow’s loss pared to 127.38 points, or 0.2 percent. The early-session wrap, in quotes timed 15:42 GMT—10:42 a.m. ET—runs the same order an hour into the session: the Nasdaq 100 up 1.57 percent at 27,046.81, the Nasdaq Composite up 1.36 percent at 24,644.52, the S&P 500 up 0.74 percent at 7,408.36, and the Dow down 0.06 percent at 51,489.99, with information technology leading the S&P’s sectors at up 1.57 percent and consumer staples last, down 0.70 percent. Nvidia rose about 6 percent in early trading, and the semiconductor fund that fell by double digits on Thursday rose about 6.5 percent. The volatility index fell about 15 percent to 23.9 in one morning account. These are snapshots an hour into a session, printed as snapshots; Thursday’s closes stand beneath them, and what the bounce is worth belongs to the close.

Europe did not get the bounce, and its midday is the session’s plainest contrast. Reuters’ European file had the STOXX 600 down 1 percent at 648.83 by 0919 GMT, its gains for the week wiped out, with media, health care, and personal and household goods each down more than 2 percent and Teleperformance down 18 percent on a cut outlook. The London midday account, at 1219 GMT, runs the fall deeper: the STOXX 600 down 1.76 percent at 643, Germany down 2.44 percent, the United Kingdom down 2.21 percent, France down 1.76 percent, Italy down 1.23 percent, and Spain down 1.25 percent. A third account puts the STOXX 600 down 1.6 percent at 644.72 at its low. The three readings were taken at three hours of one falling session and are printed as a range, 1.0 to 1.76 percent. The shelter the overnight edition noted—Europe’s smaller share of the AI trade—held in degree and not in direction: the fall is a fraction of Tokyo’s 6 percent and Seoul’s 6 percent, and it is a fall, on the day the American technology shares themselves were recovering.

The Rate Reading: Three in Four for December

The payrolls moved the rate file further than the stock file. The ten-year Treasury yield rose about 3 to 4 basis points on the report, to 4.87–4.88 percent, and the dollar index rose 0.62 percent to about 102.22 in the post-report account. The CME FedWatch probability of a 25-basis-point increase at the Federal Reserve’s December 8–9 meeting rose to 76.8 percent after the release, from above 66 percent on Thursday, per the yields account carrying the CNBC reading and the jobs-and-rates account; a later state of the same tool runs at about 77 percent. The Fed’s range stands at 3.75 to 4.00 percent, held on October 28 by 10–2, with Governor Cook and Cleveland’s President Hammack preferring an increase. The next bearing is printed on the calendar: October consumer prices on Tuesday, November 10, and the November payrolls on December 4. Two Fed officials speak this afternoon, after this edition collects; their words belong to the Evening Watch.

Gold fell on the same figures, for the second session in a row. Spot gold stood at $4,048.97 an ounce at 0124 ET, down 1 percent, before the report, and at $4,047.10 after it, down 1 percent in the Reuters figures carried in the precious-metals update, with silver edging higher; the post-report account above runs gold at about $4,050, down 1.20 percent, with the dollar and yields up. The metal stands about 4 to 4.5 percent higher on the week even after two falling sessions, below Thursday’s two-week high of $4,146. The accounts give one reason in both directions: a labor market this firm gives the central bank room to raise rates, and higher rates are the weather gold does not like.

Oil Seesaws: Over a Hundred Before Breakfast, Under It by the London Morning

Brent crossed $100 for the second morning in a row and, for the second morning, did not hold it. The overnight states stand as Edition No. 10 printed them: $99.58 at 0504 GMT and $99.90 at 0730 GMT. A Mumbai account of the Asian morning puts Brent at $100.30, up 2 percent, at 0439 GMT in its figures, with West Texas Intermediate at $91.80. The later states run down. Dow Jones Newswires’ update, timed 0602 ET, has front-month Brent down 0.7 percent at $97.59 and West Texas Intermediate down 0.5 percent at $89.98. Reuters’ London file has January Brent down 74 cents, or 0.8 percent, at $97.55 by 0826 GMT, and West Texas Intermediate down 73 cents at $89.79. Thursday’s settlement stands beneath all of it: Brent $98.29, West Texas Intermediate $90.52.

The week’s bearing is where the files disagree, and the desk prints the disagreement. The London Reuters file puts Brent on track for a fall of 16 percent on the week—its steepest weekly percentage fall since the start of the pandemic, and its biggest in absolute terms in data back to 1988—with West Texas Intermediate down more than 13 percent. The Asian and overnight files put both benchmarks at about 12 percent on the week. The difference is the contract and the hour each file measures from, and it is printed rather than resolved. What no file disputes is the cargo in the price: de-escalation hopes after the election pulling down, tanker attacks at a near-record pace in the British agency’s count holding a floor, flows through the strait under 60 percent of capacity, and JPMorgan’s surplus estimate—supply ahead of demand by 1.1 million barrels a day in September and 1.4 million in October—standing against the rebound. Saudi Aramco on Thursday cut the December price of its Arab Light crude to Asia by $2 a barrel, per the Dow Jones update, the sellers’ own reading of the same market.

The Count at Noon: Mississippi Widens, Colorado Stands, Nothing Is Called

No race was called in the morning, in either chamber, in any state—the third morning running that sentence has led this section. The Senate stands at 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans, with Alaska and Mississippi uncalled in the Associated Press Senate file, which now lists Mississippi at 100 percent of precincts reporting and Alaska at 73.95 percent. The House moved at the edges. The wire’s national tracker in its latest state shows 249 seats won by the Democrats and 12 led, against 156 won and 18 led for the Republicans. The live results file, in its update of November 6 at 09:56 CET, runs the called figure higher: 253 House seats called for the Democrats and 157 for the Republicans, with 25 still uncalled. A third tally, updated at 3:55 a.m. EST, runs it higher still: 254 called for the Democrats and 160 for the Republicans, with 414 of 435 races called. Three methods, three hours, one chamber—and agreement, as on every morning of this count, on the outcome and on nothing smaller.

Mississippi’s margin widened in the newest tally, and the widening is the count’s one correction of substance. Decision Desk HQ’s update of November 6 at 03:29 EST, carried in the live results file, puts the Democrat, Scott Colom, at 467,233 votes and the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, at 465,146—a lead of 2,087, with more than 95 percent of the estimated vote counted, the third candidate’s total revised down in the same update. The third tally above runs the same order narrower: Colom 466,877, Hyde-Smith 464,993, a lead of 1,884. The range this paper has printed for this race now runs from a few dozen votes in its earliest states to 2,087 in its newest, the leader the same in every state of it. The procedure stands as filed: affidavit identification due November 10, counties certify by November 13, the most votes wins, no automatic recount. Alaska stands exactly where it stood: the Democrat, Mary Peltola, ahead of the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, by 637 first-choice votes, 102,962 to 102,325, with the ranked-choice tabulation set for November 18.

Colorado’s 4th District corrected its totals upward on both sides, and the margin corrected with them. The overnight edition, following the state file updated Thursday evening, carried the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, at 184,103 votes and the incumbent Republican, Lauren Boebert, at 181,079—a margin of 3,024. The wire’s district file in its latest state carries both totals higher—Laubacher 184,624, Boebert 181,555, at 97.22 percent of precincts reporting and an estimated 97.3 percent of the vote—and the margin at 3,069, outside the roughly 920 votes that would require an automatic recount. The race is uncalled. What the morning added is the trailing campaign’s position: the account of the Boebert campaign’s statement records that the campaign is investigating what it calls unusual voting patterns, that its lawyer’s statement late Thursday insinuated a recount is forthcoming, and that under state law a recount at a margin above half a percent is paid for by the candidate who asks for it. The same account runs the lead at 2,927 in its own figures. The ballots that remain are signature cures and military and overseas ballots, due by November 12, with the counties finishing on November 13.

The Official Statements: A Big Agreement in Washington, No Details in Moscow

The president’s Thursday statement on Ukraine stands at noon with the Kremlin’s Friday answer beside it, and the two do not describe the same amount of knowledge. On Thursday, after meeting President Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House, the president told reporters the sides were “very close” and, in the account of the meeting, that “it’s going to be a deal, it’s going to be a big deal” that could involve more than Ukraine and “all of Europe.” He gave no terms and no timeline, said he could not say what he and Dmitriev had discussed, and said he had not met the Ukrainian delegation that was also at the White House, for an event hosted by the first lady marking the six-day humanitarian ceasefire around Oleshky, which ran from October 27 to November 1 and has expired. On Friday the Kremlin spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, was asked about the agreement in Moscow. The account of his answer records it in three words—“there are no details”—and the rest of it: Dmitriev has not yet returned from the United States and has not reported to President Putin, and Russia has received no European ideas on security guarantees. American officials held discussions in Brussels the same day with Ukraine, NATO, and European partners on security guarantees, per the account of the meeting. Delegations from Washington, Moscow, and Kyiv are due in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11. Until one of the capitals puts terms on paper, the big agreement exists as the president’s description of it, with the other capital’s spokesman stating, on the record, that he has not been told what it is.

On Iran, no decision was announced by noon, and the strait file grew by claims. The president’s Thursday words stand where the overnight edition left them—a decision coming soon, no date named—and no announcement had followed by 1200. What arrived in the morning was Tehran’s. The Revolutionary Guards said on Friday that two more oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines while crossing the strait by an unauthorized route, that both vessels had turned off their navigation and identification systems, that the strait remains closed until the United States meets Iran’s seven conditions, and that a naval electronic warfare unit took control of two uncrewed combat drones and landed them undamaged, per the agency account of the statement and the account carrying the statement’s text. No vessel was named, and no statement from the American military or any tanker operator appears in any file the desk took in the morning; the claims are filed as claims, beside the British agency’s standing count of at least five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday. The account of the president’s options runs them at four—a full resumption of the war, one large strike and an exit, continued pressure, or an interim deal on the Qatari track—with Kharg Island’s energy infrastructure named as the step Washington has not taken. The Qatari draft and Tehran’s seven conditions stand as the overnight edition printed them. Nothing was signed.

Washington’s own paper at noon is a deadline kept and a letter sent. Candidates for the House Republican leadership elections were required to declare by noon today, and no new name entered the field in the morning in any file on the shelf. The contest for minority leader stands as filed: Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, declared since Wednesday, with Speaker Mike Johnson not seeking the post; Majority Whip Tom Emmer seeking to remain whip, challenged by August Pfluger; the elections set for Tuesday, November 10. Mr. Scalise’s other act of the week reached print Friday: the account of his Thursday letter records that he asked Republican committee chairs to take inventory of the administration—to identify, in advance, the subjects the incoming majority’s investigations are expected to reach—while his own letter seeking the leadership calls for unity and for procedural disruption of the majority’s agenda. Mr. Jordan’s letter to his colleagues pitches him as battle-tested in the investigations to come. Both men are campaigning, in writing, for the job of leading the minority against the oversight the other letter is cataloguing. The House itself returns Monday.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, the Ukraine agreement: “very close” and “big” in the president’s Thursday words, “no details” in the Kremlin spokesman’s Friday words, with the envoy who carried whatever was discussed not yet home to report it—two capitals describing one meeting, and the distance between the descriptions is the fact. Second, the House at noon: 249 seats won in the wire’s tracker, 253 called in the live file’s morning check, 254 called in the third tally, with the uncalled running at 25 in one file and 21 in another. Third, Brent’s week: down about 12 percent in the Asian and overnight files, down 16 percent in the London file, the steepest since the pandemic in that file’s measure—one falling market read from two starting lines. Fourth, Mississippi: 1,884 in one tally and 2,087 in the newest, the lead widening in both directions of the comparison and the leader unchanged in every bearing this paper has ever printed for the race. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts of the midday are single-valued: payrolls rose 165,000 and unemployment fell to 4.1 percent; September is revised to 60,000; the December hike probability stands above 76 percent; Brent trades under $100 and gold under $4,050; Europe is down between 1.0 and 1.76 percent at its midday; no race was called; two more tankers are claimed in the strait and none is confirmed; and the Abu Dhabi delegations meet on November 10, the same day the House conferences elect their leaders and Mississippi’s affidavit deadline falls. The session belongs to the close. The log proceeds to the evening.

### The Offer and the Answer: What the Ballot Box Did to the Tax Base

Filed as: Breaking Report — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-06T11:45:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-06-offer-and-answer.html

Breaking Report

 The Infrastructure File — The Tax Base and the Ballot

 Objective

 The Offer and the Answer: What the Ballot Box Did to the Tax Base

 On November 3 the voters limited the data-center buildout in forty of forty-one local decisions. The offers those decisions answered are also in the record: the tax revenue projected, the jobs counted, and the one county that said yes for twenty-five years and now collects $1.2 billion a year. The desk files the two records side by side.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1145 ET, Friday, November 6, 2026.

 

The News in the File

Ballotpedia records 41 local ballot measures on data-center policy in ten states, tallied after the election: on 28 a yes vote would limit development through bans or moratoriums, and on 13 a yes vote would facilitate it. Voters approved 27 of the limiting measures and defeated all 13 of the facilitating ones. The single exception is Harwood, North Dakota, which defeated a measure adding review requirements to industrial projects.

Ohio held twenty-one of the forty-one measures in eighteen municipalities, and the margins were not narrow. By the Cincinnati Enquirer’s accounting, eleven municipalities passed outright bans, among them Trenton, at 80 percent to 20 percent, and Sunbury, where a charter amendment banning facilities of 25 megawatts or more passed with 78.6 percent. In Perry, more than 87 percent approved financial-guarantee requirements on incentivized developers. In Wilmington, below, about 80 percent rejected each of four rezonings. Six measures decided earlier in 2026 had already run the same way: Canterbury, New Hampshire, prohibited data centers in March, 322 to 63; Monterey Park, California, in June, 10,388 to 1,372; Augusta Township, Michigan, overturned a rezoning in August, 2,314 to 269.

The ballot measures are the counted part of a larger record. Fortune counted at least 138 Ohio municipalities and townships with active moratoriums as of September 17; the National Conference of State Legislatures found lawmakers in at least 28 of the 38 states offering data-center tax incentives pursuing rollbacks this year; Data Center Watch counted some $68 billion of projects blocked or delayed in the second quarter of 2026 alone. What follows is the other half of the file: the fiscal record of the places doing the voting, the terms of the offers they answered, and the realized record of the places that answered the other way. Figures from adopted budgets and legislative audits are printed as record; figures from developers of unbuilt projects, as company figures.

The Offer, Measured

The most complete audit of what a data center offers a locality was made in Virginia, and its job count is modest. Industry representatives told the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, the General Assembly’s oversight arm, reporting on December 9, 2024, that a typical 250,000-square-foot data center employs approximately 50 full-time workers, about half of them contract workers. Construction is the larger employment event: a building takes twelve to eighteen months to raise, with approximately 1,500 workers on site at the peak, and the jobs tend to be high-paying. Statewide, the commission estimated the industry contributes 74,000 jobs and $9.1 billion in gross domestic product each year, most of the benefit deriving from construction. A Brookings study of counties receiving a first large data center found private employment up 4 to 5 percent over five to six years; estimates ignoring pre-existing trends overstate the effect by about three times.

The revenue side of the audit is larger than the jobs side, and varies by two orders of magnitude between localities. In the five Virginia localities with relatively mature data-center markets, data-center revenue ranged from less than 1 percent of total local revenue to 31 percent. The commission’s sentence on the geography of the benefit is printed as written: localities in economically distressed areas of the state could benefit from data centers through increased local tax revenue, but these localities could have difficulty attracting the industry. Against the revenue stand the incentives: states forgo more than $3 billion a year to data-center tax exemptions, by Good Jobs First’s estimate, and the commission put Virginia’s return on its own sales-tax exemption at about 48 cents recovered per dollar forgone.

Wilmington, Ohio: Four Votes on 546 Acres

Wilmington is a city of 12,802 people in Clinton County, in the farm country between Cincinnati and Columbus. Census figures (2020–2024 American Community Survey) put median household income at $57,199, against $80,734 nationally, and 17.5 percent of residents in poverty; Clinton County stands higher, at $70,407 and 11.9 percent. The city’s modern history has one large event in it. Its air park was the national sorting hub of Airborne Express and then of DHL; when DHL ended its United States domestic delivery service in 2009, the hub closed, at a loss the Greater Ohio Policy Center puts at 16,000 jobs in the area. Air cargo returned in time—Amazon Air operates at the air park today—and the population stands 138 above its 2020 count.

Two data-center rezonings reached Wilmington in 2026, and only one of them reached the voters. On September 3 the council, acting by emergency ordinances effective immediately and not subject to referendum under Ohio law, rezoned the 471-acre Cosler Farm on U.S. 68 for a proposed $4 billion Amazon Web Services campus of about 1.9 million square feet. Separately, the council rezoned four parcels, about 546 acres, from rural residential to light industrial for a project of Ardent, affiliated with TAC Data Centers; the four would have taken the city’s land zoned for data centers from about 500 acres to more than 1,000. A residents’ group collected 1,529 signatures in about twenty-five days and placed the four on the ballot. On November 3, each was rejected by about 80 percent of the voters; the first ordinance drew 739 in favor and 2,885 against, in the Wilmington News Journal’s county totals, unofficial pending certification. The four parcels remain rural residential. The emergency rezoning was not decided on November 3 and is not affected by the vote.

Three Michigan Townships

Augusta Township, in Washtenaw County southeast of Ann Arbor, is a farming community of 7,345 people, and its census figures are not a distressed place’s figures. The Census Bureau puts its median household income at $108,457, above its county’s $89,180. In July 2025 the board voted unanimously, against its own planning commission’s recommendation, to rezone 522 acres of farmland for a Thor Equities data center reported at $1 billion; officials pointed at the time to millions of dollars a year in new tax revenue for the township and its schools. Opponents needed 561 signatures to force a vote and turned in nearly twice that within about a month. On August 4, 2026, the voters overturned the rezoning, 2,314 to 269. Residents have since filed petitions to recall the board members who approved it.

Delhi Township, south of Lansing, answered an offer that had not yet become an application. The township has 28,431 people, a median household income of $90,437, per the Census Bureau’s tables, and, by the Lansing State Journal’s account, annual tax revenue of $23 million; a twelve-month moratorium adopted in April runs to April 2027. On October 27 the Lansing Economic Area Partnership and Lighthouse Sustainability, a Colorado developer, announced a proposed 700-megawatt data center on 423 acres, an investment stated above $10 billion, without prior consultation with the township, by the manager’s statement. The sponsors’ projections were township tax revenue more than tripling, $23 million a year to $76 million, with $16 million a year added to the Holt and Mason schools, a $20 million community fund, and a no-cost residential solar program. On October 28 the township withdrew from the partnership. On October 30, three days after the announcement, the board voted 6 to 0 to record its opposition to any data center development in the township. No application had been filed.

Saline Township, twenty miles south of Augusta, said no and was answered in court. It is a farming community of about 2,375 people; a policy study of the case puts its annual budget at roughly $1 million. Related Digital proposed a multi-building campus there for Oracle and OpenAI on about 575 acres. On September 10, 2025, the board voted 4 to 1 to deny the rezoning; the developer sued two days later; on October 15 a consent judgment rezoned the site and bound the township to approve a twelve-year, 50 percent tax abatement whose final value awaits the State Tax Commission. The settlement’s tax-exemption form lists $1.31 billion of real property and $3.5 billion of equipment, $4.81 billion in all. The company’s 2026 statements value the project above $43 billion and put the resulting tax revenue, after the abatement, at about $147 million a year to county, schools, and township—well north of $150 million a year for the better part of two decades, in Oracle’s release—with more than 2,500 union construction jobs and about 450 permanent on-site jobs, all company figures. Construction began June 1, 2026; by late September the company reported one million union craft hours worked. The township’s share, the company states, is more than 2,000 times what the land would have yielded as farmland.

The Places That Said Yes

Pike County, Ohio, holds the poorest census figures in this file, and it signed the largest agreement in it. The county, in the Appalachian foothills, has 27,061 people, 27 below its 2020 count; the Census Bureau puts median household income at $52,736 and 19.1 percent of residents in poverty. Its largest site is the decommissioned Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion Plant, whose cleanup has employed the county for a generation. On August 17, 2026, SB Energy, OpenAI, and Nvidia announced the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus on that ground: SB Energy will build, own, and operate the campus and lease approximately eight gigawatts of capacity to OpenAI for twenty years, with Nvidia the exclusive supplier of the computing infrastructure and $1.5 billion invested in SB Energy. The companies’ stated terms are 35,000 construction jobs across a six-year buildout through 2032 and 2,500 long-term operating jobs, capacity phased from 2028, the developer paying the full cost of the grid upgrades required, at least $4.2 billion of regional grid infrastructure built with AEP Ohio, and community funds of $40 million from each company. Every figure in this paragraph is a company projection attached to an agreement signed in August. Pike County’s permanent-jobs figure, 2,500 across eight gigawatts, stands beside the Virginia auditors’ figure for one typical facility, about fifty; the difference is the difference between a campus and a building.

Massena, New York, voted the other way on the only question put to it, by three votes to two. The town, on the St. Lawrence River, has 12,058 people; the Census Bureau puts its median household income at $54,595 and its poverty rate at 23.1 percent, the highest in this file. Its industrial ground is the former Alcoa East and Reynolds Metals site, shuttered aluminum works. North Country Colocation Services, an affiliate of the New York Digital Investment Group, proposes a 1.5-million-square-foot data center there; the company states about 200 permanent jobs, and construction estimates run from 1,800 to 2,500 workers over about two years. On September 16 the town board voted 3 to 2 against a six-month moratorium; the proposal proceeds without the pause its opponents petitioned for. Over the project stands a state question: the governor’s July 14 executive order paused state environmental permits for large data centers for up to a year; the developer states the project is exempt, and state officials have not confirmed it.

In Hermantown, Minnesota, the terms changed before the answer did. On October 30, after two meetings halted by protests and four hours of testimony running mostly against the project, the city council voted unanimously to approve a Google campus of about 1.7 million square feet and some 500 megawatts of demand. Before the vote, Google had withdrawn a request for up to $80 million in property tax abatements, reduced the project from four buildings to three, and signed a decommissioning agreement valued at $210 million. The Hermantown and Delhi sequences closed in the same week. In Delhi, the answer came three days after an announcement and before any application. In Hermantown, it came after the abatement request was withdrawn.

Loudoun County: The Realized Record

One county in the record has run the experiment to completion, and its figures are budget figures, not projections. Loudoun County, Virginia, the largest data-center market in the world, has 449,749 people, up from 312,311 in 2010; the Census Bureau puts its median household income at $181,765, the highest county figure in the nation, and its poverty rate at 4.3 percent. In fiscal 2026, by the county’s own published figures, data centers generated $1.2 billion in real and personal property tax revenue, 39 percent of the county’s overall budget. The adopted fiscal 2027 budget projects about $1.3 billion, roughly 45 percent of local tax revenue and 38 percent of the general fund by budget analyses; of the total, about $417 million is real property tax and about $879 million is personal property tax on the equipment inside the buildings, taxed at $4.15 per $100 of value. The county has cut its homeowner real property rate every year for ten years, $1.145 per $100 in 2016 to $0.805 in 2026, and attributes the cuts to the data-center revenue; its budget office states that without the industry the rate would likely exceed one dollar. In 2023 the county created a Revenue Stabilization Fund, against the stated risk that data-center revenue falls short of the budget built on it.

The county that collects the revenue has also begun, in the same years, to close the door it opened. On March 18, 2025, the Board of Supervisors voted 7 to 2 to end by-right development; new projects require a special exception. In September 2026 the board voted 7 to 1 to 1 to draft a twelve-month pause on new data-center and substation applications. The two halves of the national record meet in these figures and are printed together, without a sentence between them: Loudoun County’s median household income is $181,765, and it is drafting a pause. Wilmington’s median household income is $57,199, its poverty rate is 17.5 percent, and it voted four times, by about four to one, to keep 546 acres in rural residential zoning. Massena’s poverty rate is 23.1 percent, and its board voted 3 to 2 to let a proposal proceed. Pike County’s poverty rate is 19.1 percent, and its ground holds a signed agreement for eight gigawatts. The log proceeds to the Evening Watch.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. The national count carries one: Ballotpedia’s verified list holds 41 measures decided on November 3, another tracker lists 47 for the same day, the inclusion rules separating the lists are not published, and the desk prints Ballotpedia’s 41 with the range noted. The DHL figure carries one: the Greater Ohio Policy Center puts the 2009 loss at 16,000 jobs in the area, while county accounts describe thousands eliminated; the desk prints the policy center’s figure as its figure. Saline Township carries the widest triangle in the file: the settlement’s filing values the project at $4.81 billion, the company’s 2026 statements above $43 billion, the $147 million annual tax figure is the company’s arithmetic, the abatement it assumes has not received its final value from the State Tax Commission, and the division of the revenue among county, schools, and township has not been published. Two categories of number run through this report and are not interchangeable: Delhi’s $76 million and Pike County’s 35,000 construction jobs are sponsor projections for unbuilt projects, the second stated across a six-year buildout without a statement of whether it counts positions or job-years; Loudoun’s $1.2 billion is an adopted budget’s accounting of money collected. The Ohio results are unofficial until the county boards certify them. Against the triangle, the single-valued facts stand: the votes were cast as counted above; the census figures are the bureau’s; the Virginia audit’s typical facility employs about fifty people; and in every locality in this file, the offer and the answer are both matters of public record.

 The Clippings Filed With This Report

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Fourteen items.

 

 SubjectiveJoint Legislative Audit and Review Commission—Data Centers in VirginiaThe General Assembly’s audit of the industry, dated December 9, 2024: a typical 250,000-square-foot facility employs about fifty full-time workers, about half of them contractors; construction peaks near 1,500 workers per building over twelve to eighteen months; the industry contributes an estimated 74,000 jobs and $9.1 billion in gross domestic product statewide, mostly from construction; in five mature localities data-center revenue ran from under 1 percent to 31 percent of total local revenue; and distressed localities could benefit from the tax revenue but could have difficulty attracting the industry.

### The Distributed Machine: Redundancy Becomes the Architecture

Filed as: Breaking Report — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-06T11:05:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-06-distributed-machine.html

Breaking Report

 The Infrastructure File — The Architecture of the Data Center

 Objective

 The Distributed Machine: Redundancy Becomes the Architecture

 Telephony and computing began in single rooms, served through hierarchies. A century of automation, copying, and routing moved the service into the network itself. The record runs from the La Porte exchange of 1892 to the availability zones of 2026, and it lands on a buildout now contested site by site.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1105 ET, Friday, November 6, 2026.

 

The News in the File

The newest data-center plan in the record is not a campus. It is a scatter. Trade accounts filed on Friday, November 6, reported that Nvidia is examining a plan with the fiber carrier Brightspeed to place small data centers in more than 130 former telephone buildings across the United States—sites that already hold power connections and fiber—for a combined capacity reported at up to one gigawatt. Inside the project, according to the same accounts, the arrangement is described as an inference network: computing placed in many small facilities near the people requesting it, rather than in a few large ones far away. The companies have issued no announcement; the desk files the item as reported, and grades it again in the cocked hat below. The plan is filed here because of its shape. The shape is the subject of this report: the industry’s unit of construction is changing from the building to the network.

The counts describe the same change at the largest scale. Synergy Research Group counted 1,297 operational hyperscale data centers worldwide in late 2025, nearly triple the number of early 2018, with 770 more in planning, construction, or fit-out. Amazon Web Services operates 38 regions; Microsoft closed 2025 with more than 70 Azure regions and more than 400 data centers; Google Cloud stood at 42 regions and 127 zones. The facilities differ in size and owner. The architecture they share is the point: capacity held in many places at once, data copied between them as a matter of routine, and no single address at which the service lives.

The Single Room: Computing as It Began

Commercial computing began as one machine in one room, and the room was the service. IBM announced the System/360 family in April 1964, a line of compatible mainframes on which a customer’s programs could run across models. The machines stood in air-conditioned rooms, attended by operators, and the work arrived as decks of cards and left as printed paper. Time-sharing, added to the line with the Model 67 in 1966, let many users work at the same machine in the same hour. The user’s furniture was a terminal: in the 1970s, characteristically, an IBM 3270 display—a screen and keyboard with no computing of its own, which collected a full screen of entries and sent it to the mainframe when the operator pressed Enter. The arrangement was efficient and entirely dependent. A mainframe of the period could serve thousands of terminal users, and every one of them was served from the single room, or not at all.

Telephony began the same way, in a single room of a different kind. In the manual exchange, every call passed through an operator seated at a cord board, who took the request by voice and completed the connection by hand, plugging one cord into the jack of the calling line and another into the jack of the called line. The network above the local board was arranged as a hierarchy of five classes of office, from the Class 5 end office that served subscribers up through toll and primary and sectional centers to the Class 1 regional centers; tandem offices connected end offices to one another and to the levels above. The system’s research arm, Bell Telephone Laboratories, began moving to Murray Hill, New Jersey, in 1941; the transistor was demonstrated at Murray Hill in 1947. The hierarchy was orderly and it was a chain: each level depended on the level above it, and the operator’s hands were the switching fabric of the whole.

The Operator Leaves the Path

The first break in the chain was mechanical. Almon Strowger’s step-by-step switch, patented in 1891, let the caller’s own dial pulses move the switch directly, digit by digit, with no operator in the path. The first commercial step-by-step exchange opened at La Porte, Indiana, on November 3, 1892. The Bell System’s crossbar switch followed: the No. 1 Crossbar was installed at the Troy Avenue office in Brooklyn in 1938, and the No. 5 Crossbar, first installed at Media, Pennsylvania, in 1948, became the workhorse of the system. In 1965 the No. 1 Electronic Switching System put a stored program—a computer—in charge of the connections. Each step removed a pair of hands and a single point of attention from the path of a call. Switching became a function the network performed on itself, in every office at once, and the five-class hierarchy flattened as the offices grew able to reach one another directly.

The lesson the telephone network taught was structural, and computing learned it twice. A service concentrated in one room fails with the room. A service performed by a hierarchy fails at the level that fails. The systems that replaced both arrangements distributed the work itself—first the switching, then the content, then the computing—until the service no longer had a single address at which it could be interrupted.

The CDN Turn: Copies Near the Reader

The distribution of content began as an answer to a crowd. In 1995 Tim Berners-Lee challenged colleagues at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology to solve the congestion of a popular web site—the flash crowd that arrived at one server at one address and overwhelmed it. Tom Leighton, an MIT professor of applied mathematics, and Daniel Lewin, his graduate student, answered with consistent hashing, a method of spreading content across many servers so that the set could grow, shrink, and lose members without re-mapping the whole. Akamai Technologies was incorporated on August 20, 1998, by Leighton and Lewin with Jonathan Seelig and Randall Kaplan. The name is the Hawaiian word akamai: intelligent, clever—colloquially, cool.

The content delivery network changed where a web page lives. Under the Akamai model, copies of a publisher’s content are held on servers placed inside many networks, near the readers. A request is answered by a nearby copy. The publisher’s origin server remains, but it is no longer the place the public visits; it is the place the copies are made from. The failure arithmetic changed with the geography: a server under a flash crowd is one copy among many, and a server that fails removes one copy, not the publication. Within its first years Akamai was, by the accounts of the period, effectively the content delivery industry; the architecture it sold—many copies, served locally, refreshed from an origin—became the default shape of the public web.

The Modern Form: Zones, Regions, and One Address Everywhere

The hyperscalers applied the same principle to computing itself, and wrote it into their operating instructions. Amazon Web Services divides its infrastructure into Regions, each physically and logically independent, and each Region into three or more Availability Zones. An Availability Zone is one or more discrete data centers, physically separated from the zones beside it, with independent power, cooling, and network connections. AWS’s published reliability guidance instructs customers to deploy production workloads across at least two zones and to replicate data between them; the zones sit close enough for synchronous replication at single-digit-millisecond latency, so a copy is current, not eventual. Several of the company’s largest storage and database services replicate across zones by default. The design objective, in the document’s own terms, is the avoidance of single points of failure, including the underlying physical infrastructure.

Cloudflare carries the principle into the network’s addressing. Its network runs on anycast: every location announces the same IP addresses, and the internet’s routing delivers each request to the nearest location able to answer it. Cloudflare’s own documentation states the failure behavior plainly: because multiple nodes advertise the same address, if one node fails, requests are routed to another node in close proximity. There is no failover address to publish and no single facility whose loss changes the address of the service. The company reports data centers in 335 cities. The service is the address; the address is everywhere the network is.

The storage industry had named the underlying principle a generation earlier, and the facility now follows the disk. RAID arrays, standardized in the late 1980s, write data across multiple disks so that the failure of one disk is an event, not a loss; backup practice added copies held in different places against the failure of the building itself. The desk prints the analogy as an analogy, because it is exact at the level of design: the unit of engineering is no longer the single store of the data but the set of copies, the rules that keep them in agreement, and the routing that finds a surviving copy when one is gone. A modern data center is built the way the array was: replaceable, replicated, and one member of a set.

The Contested Ground, and the Structural Answer

The construction program is contested at the level of the individual site, and the record of the contest is counted. On November 3, voters in ten states decided 41 local measures on data-center construction; in Ballotpedia’s complete tracker, 40 went the way of tighter limits. Data Center Watch, as reported by Data Center Knowledge, counted more than 36 projects representing $162 billion of investment blocked or significantly delayed as of June 2025. Site selection has adjusted its vocabulary to the record: an industry account of 2026 practice describes the discipline as deliverability—the overlap of entitled land, available power, and a local community willing to partner on the project—and describes the market splitting into two tracks, hyperscale campuses of hundreds of megawatts and hyperlocal sites of one to twenty megawatts close to users.

Distribution is the architecture’s answer to a refusal, and the answer is mechanical rather than rhetorical. A workload deployed across zones and regions under the operators’ own published guidance does not have a hometown. Capacity refused in one jurisdiction is capacity placed in another; a site that is delayed delays one member of a set whose other members continue. The reported Nvidia–Brightspeed plan is the limiting case of the same logic: capacity distributed across more than 130 existing buildings, each individually small, each already holding the power and fiber connections a new campus waits years to obtain, and none of them individually the network. The data center began as a palace built to hold a unique machine. The record of 2026 shows it completing the telephone network’s migration: from the single room, to the hierarchy, to the network of copies—a service that persists because no one place is the service.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. The scale figures carry one. The desk’s sources put Amazon’s footprint at 38 regions with 120 availability zones in one October 2026 accounting and at 38 regions with more than 100 zones in another; the counts were taken at different dates against a buildout adding zones continuously, and they agree on the structure while differing on the count. The Friday item carries a wider triangle: the Nvidia–Brightspeed plan rests on trade reporting that the companies have not confirmed in any announcement the desk can file, and its figures—130 buildings, one gigawatt—are the reported figures of a plan under examination, not of a construction program under way. The historical bearings are single-valued: the La Porte exchange opened on November 3, 1892; Akamai was incorporated on August 20, 1998; the No. 1 Crossbar went in at Brooklyn in 1938. The architecture those dates produced is the single-valued fact underneath the triangle of counts: the copies are the system now. The log proceeds to the Midday Watch.

 The Clippings Filed With This Report

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Eight items.

 

 SubjectiveAmazon Web Services — deploy the workload to multiple locationsThe operator’s own reliability guidance: each Region physically and logically independent and made of three or more Availability Zones; zones physically separated and isolated, with independent power and network; data replicated synchronously between zones; production workloads to run in at least two zones; the stated design principle is the avoidance of single points of failure, the physical infrastructure included.

 SubjectiveCloudflare — what anycast is, in the operator’s accountThe operator’s explainer of its own architecture: one IP address applied to many servers, queries answered by the closest, availability preserved when a resolver goes offline because others answer, and the network stated at 335 cities. The desk’s report takes the mechanism and the failure behavior from this account and prints the city count as the operator’s own figure.

 SubjectiveData Center Knowledge — the hyperscalers in 2026The trade paper’s state of the buildout: 1,297 operational hyperscale data centers counted by Synergy Research Group in late 2025 and 770 in the pipeline; Amazon at 38 regions, Microsoft past 70 regions and 400 data centers, Google at 42 regions and 127 zones; and Data Center Watch’s count of more than 36 projects, $162 billion of investment, blocked or significantly delayed as of June 2025.

 SubjectiveSoftonic — the reported Nvidia and Brightspeed planFriday’s account of the reported plan: more than 130 former telecom buildings to be used as small data centers, reusing sites that already have power and fiber, the portfolio reaching about one gigawatt, and the arrangement described inside the project as an inference network for live requests close to users. The item is reported rather than announced, and the report above files it as such.

 SubjectiveKnowledge at Wharton — Akamai’s foundingThe business school’s account of the company’s start: the name Hawaiian for intelligent and clever; the product a mathematical algorithm, developed at MIT under Tom Leighton, routing content to servers that forward it to the end user; the company founded by Leighton with Daniel Lewin, his graduate student, after Tim Berners-Lee’s challenge on internet congestion.

 SubjectiveTelephone World — the switch timelineThe dated record of the switching succession: the Strowger switch patented in 1891 and its first commercial exchange at La Porte, Indiana, on November 3, 1892; the first No. 1 Crossbar at Brooklyn in 1938; crossbar tandem in 1941; the No. 5 Crossbar at Media, Pennsylvania, in 1948. The report’s automation dates are taken from this file.

 SubjectiveRoute Fifty — voters reject data centers in local initiativesThe election account of the local votes: more than forty measures across ten states, the opponents of data-center development successful in virtually all of them, Ohio carrying the most initiatives, some votes advisory rather than binding, and a single locality where the facilities prevailed. Ballotpedia’s complete count, forty-one measures and forty for tighter limits, is the figure the report prints.

 SubjectiveInflect — site selection in 2026An industry account of how sites are now chosen: the field splitting into hyperscale campuses of hundreds of megawatts and hyperlocal sites of one to twenty megawatts; deliverability defined as the overlap of entitled land, available power, and a community willing to partner; and demand pushing activity into secondary markets as primary markets fill.
